Volume 09 · Chapter 06

Factor models and empirical asset pricing

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v09-c05

By the endEstimate factor exposures and distinguish explanatory fits from investable premiums.

Capability and prerequisites

You can estimate factor exposures, derive a precisely stated factor-pricing restriction, and decide whether an apparent premium is a descriptive statistic, a priced risk exposure or an implementable trading result. You can construct a factor using information available before investment and carry its holdings, funding and costs through a complete cash ledger. The central discipline is to keep those different claims separate.

Use state prices and stochastic discount factors, covariance and residual diversification, CAPM and regression alpha, and least-squares projection and rank. Write R for a simple total return, Rf for the safe gross return and rf=Rf−1 for its simple return. An asset's excess return is rie=Ri−rf=Gi−Rf. Dates, currency and fee perimeter must agree before subtracting returns.

A research desk reports that two factors explain 95% of a strategy's variation. Its intercept is positive; a portfolio formed from a characteristic also earned money. Those statements do not yet establish a pricing model, a new source of compensated risk or a trade a client could have implemented. We will reconstruct what each calculation actually identifies. All numerical cases are original and synthetic. The finite-state economy, the eight-observation sample and the four-month trading record are separate teaching constructions, not a single observed dataset.

1. Define the factor before interpreting its coefficient

A factor model describes several returns using a small collection of common variables. With a K-vector of factors f, a population linear projection with an intercept is

rie = αi + βi′f + εi,   E[εi]=0,   Cov(f,εi)=0.

If factor covariance is positive definite and second moments exist, minimizing expected squared residual gives βi=Var(f)−1Cov(f,rie) and αi=E[rie]−βi′E[f]. Orthogonality follows from the minimization; it is not evidence that the residual has no economic risk. Factors need not be mutually independent or uncorrelated. Their joint covariance belongs in the calculation. A coefficient is a conditional linear exposure holding the other included factors fixed, not automatically a causal response.

Three factor contracts with different interpretations
VariableConstruction and unitsWhat its mean can mean
Traded excess returnBuy one CU of a funded asset and borrow one CU safely. Terminal payoff is G−Rf, per one CU reference notional.Expected payoff on that stated zero-initial-cost exposure; funding and costs still matter.
Long-minus-short spreadOne CU long one portfolio and one CU short another: RL−RS before separately stated costs.Expected spread payoff per reference notional, not a return obtained by dividing by zero initial equity.
Nontraded variableAn inflation surprise, production innovation or latent statistical component, in explicitly chosen units.A statistical mean. Centering it to zero does not eliminate the price of exposure to its fluctuations.

Calling all three “factor returns” hides an important difference. A macroeconomic innovation cannot be purchased by borrowing its mean. A factor-mimicking portfolio needs an actual budget, available assets and a demonstrated relationship to that innovation; correlation alone does not establish exact replication. Similarly, a principal component is chosen to explain variation under a normalization, not to establish a tradable premium or identify marginal utility.

Scaling matters. If z*=cz for a nonzero constant c, the same exposure has coefficient b*=b/c. Any consistent price of risk must become λ*=cλ, preserving bλ. An invertible rotation changes the reported coefficients and factor coordinates without changing the fitted span. Economic names require a construction and mechanism beyond this algebra.

2. Exact spanning makes a strong, testable pricing statement

For this section, assume one frictionless period, unrestricted signed positions, a safe asset, and no arbitrage. The previous chapter supplies a strictly positive SDF m satisfying E[m]=1/Rf, 1=E[mGi] for a unit-price claim, and E[mrie]=0. Let each fk be the payoff of a specified traded zero-cost factor position. It therefore satisfies E[mfk]=0. Expectations use physical probabilities; m supplies valuation weights.

Suppose a claim is exactly spanned: rie=ai+βi′f in every possible state. Multiply by m and take expectations. Zero pricing of the claim's excess payoff and all factor positions gives 0=aiE[m]. Because E[m]>0, ai=0. Consequently

E[rie] = βi′E[f]   when the payoff is exactly spanned by the safe asset and traded factors.

The trading proof is equally useful. The asset minus its safe-financed initial purchase generates rie at zero initial cost. Subtract βi units of the zero-cost factor positions. What remains is a sure ai. If it were nonzero, choose its sign to obtain a positive sure payoff at zero cost. This proof depends on exact statewise cancellation and feasible trading, not a high regression fit or a small standard error.

When fk=Gk−Rf for unit-price factor funds, the full claim payoff is Gi=ΣβikGk+(1−Σβik)Rf. The safe position closes the initial budget. Comparing two prices requires the same dated payoff; changing the purchase price changes the return and its normalization. An apparent discrepancy in two sample mean returns is not yet a replication-price discrepancy.

Worked example 1 — Exact replication and an apparently positive alpha

The Ilex synthetic economy has eight equiprobable states: independent signs U,V,E each equal ±1. Set Rf=1.02 and

m = (1/1.02)(1−U/4−V/5−E/10),   f1=0.03+0.12U,   f2=0.02+0.10V.

The smallest bracket in m is 1−0.25−0.20−0.10=0.45, so m is strictly positive. Independence and symmetry give E[m]=1/1.02, E[mf1]=(0.03−0.25×0.12)/1.02=0, and E[mf2]=(0.02−0.20×0.10)/1.02=0. Thus safe and factor-fund payoffs Gk=1.02+fk have price one. These are synthetic physical states, not empirical probabilities.

Claim A pays XA=1.02+1.5f1−0.25f2=1.06+0.18U−0.025V. Its replica holds 1.5 units of Fund 1, −0.25 of Fund 2 and −0.25 of the safe asset. Initial cost is 1.5−0.25−0.25=1; every state payoff agrees. The expected excess return at that fair price is 1.5×0.03−0.25×0.02=4%, and its expected total simple return is 6%.

Now an additional clone offers that exact same XA for 0.98. Buy one clone, short 1.5 Fund 1, buy 0.25 Fund 2 and hold 0.27 of the safe asset. Initial cost is 0.98−1.5+0.25+0.27=0. Its terminal payoff is XA−1.5G1+0.25G2+0.27×1.02=0.0204 in every state. The 0.02 saving is invested safely; the claim's full safe payoff has not been omitted. The enlarged quoted market is inconsistent with the pricing rule and admits exact arbitrage under the stated trading assumptions.

A different unit-price claim B has excess return rBe=0.004+1.5f1−0.25f2+0.04E. Its residual ε=0.04E has zero mean and zero covariance with both included factors. Yet E[mε]=−0.10×0.04/1.02. Therefore E[mrBe]=0.004/1.02−0.004/1.02=0, and its full payoff also has price one. Its factor-model intercept is 0.4%, and its expected excess return is 4.4%. Hedging the two factors leaves 0.004+0.04E: either 4.4% or −3.6% per reference CU. This is priced omitted risk, not a sure gain. The common positive SDF establishes consistency for the correctly priced claims.

3. What an approximate factor-pricing argument must assume

Return to rie=αi+βi′f+εi, with traded zero-cost factors and a zero-mean residual. Applying the pricing identity gives the exact relation

αi = −E[mεi]/E[m] = −RfCov(m,εi),   |αi| ≤ [σ(m)/E[m]] σ(εi).

The inequality follows directly from Cauchy–Schwarz. Factor orthogonality says Cov(f,ε)=0; it does not say Cov(m,ε)=0. Zero alpha follows if the residual is absent, or if an additional model implies that it is orthogonal to the SDF. For example, if m lies in the linear span of a constant and the included factors, projection orthogonality suffices. Whether that SDF specification is economically appropriate remains a pricing hypothesis.

For a sequence of diversified positions, let εN=Σwi,Nεi,N. If residuals are mutually uncorrelated and their variances are bounded by M, Var(εN)≤MΣwi,N². Equal weights give M/N. Now impose a uniform pricing restriction σ(mN)/E[mN]≤K across that sequence. Then |αN|≤K√(M/N)→0. More general weights work when their squared sum vanishes. Correlated residuals require checking the full residual covariance, and short-weight concentration need not disappear merely because the asset count grows.

This is a conditional approximate-pricing result: small aggregate residual risk plus a uniformly bounded price of risk forces small alpha. It does not say that every finite portfolio is riskless, that every individual asset's alpha is zero, or that no-arbitrage in each finite economy alone supplies the uniform bound. A nonzero probability of loss remains compatible with a very attractive mean-to-volatility ratio. Calling that a sure finite arbitrage would change the theorem.

MIT's APT teaching discussion motivates multiple systematic sources and the need to choose factors. Here the exact-spanning proof and the conditional residual bound are stated separately. APT reasoning does not by itself identify which observed variables are the correct factors. We do not claim to have proved every infinite-market formulation of the arbitrage pricing theory.

Worked example 2 — Less residual risk is still finite risk

In a separate synthetic family, E1,…,EN are independent equiprobable signs. A zero-cost claim pays zi=0.02+0.20Ei per reference CU. The equal average z̄ has mean 0.02 and residual variance 0.04/N. At N=4, its five possible payoffs, ordered by the number of positive signs, are −0.18, −0.08, 0.02, 0.12 and 0.22. Loss probability is (1+4)/16=5/16. For every finite N, the all-negative state has positive probability and payoff −0.18.

These claims can all be priced by the strictly positive product kernel mN=(1/Rf)∏(1−0.10Ej). Independence gives E[mN]=1/Rf. For a particular i, all other factors have expectation one, while E[(1−0.10Ei)(0.02+0.20Ei)]=0.02−0.02=0. Thus E[mNzi]=0 for every i. Each finite economy has a strictly positive pricing law despite the positive common mean and decreasing average variance.

There is no contradiction with the bound: E[mN²]/E[mN]2=(1.01)N, so its squared coefficient of variation is 1.01N−1, which is not uniformly bounded. By contrast, if we additionally required K=0.5, N=100 would imply |α100|≤0.5×0.20/10=1%. A 2% residual premium would violate that additional restriction. It would not prove a statewise sure gain from the original finite variance calculation. The lab reports both the actual product-kernel family and this separately labeled hypothetical bound.

4. Nontraded factors need a price of covariance risk

For a nontraded K-vector z, write a centered projection rie=μi+bi′(z−E[z])+εi, where E[εi]=0 and Cov(z,εi)=0. The SDF equation gives

μi = bi′λ − RfCov(m,εi),   λ = −RfCov(z,m).

This follows by expanding E[mrie]=0 and using E[m]=1/Rf. Centering z has no effect on its covariance or λ. The expected value of an inflation innovation may be zero by definition while its risk price is nonzero. If z is itself a vector of priced traded zero-cost factor payoffs, its pricing equation implies λ=E[z], recovering the traded-factor normalization. Without that trading contract, setting λ equal to its sample mean is unjustified.

A factor that explains much variation can have a small or zero price of risk: Cov(m,z) may be zero even when its variance is large. Conversely, a less variable component can matter greatly for prices if its covariance with m is economically important. Prediction of realized returns, statistical explanation of contemporaneous variation and explanation of cross-sectional expected returns are different tasks. A successful pricing restriction is joint with its SDF, factor set, asset universe and trading assumptions.

5. Estimate exposures before interpreting a fitted alpha

For T aligned observations, put a column of ones and K factor observations into X and the asset's corresponding excess returns into y. OLS chooses θ̂=(α̂,β̂′)′ to minimize (y−Xθ)′(y−Xθ). Differentiating gives X′Xθ̂=X′y. With full column rank, v′X′Xv=‖Xv‖²>0 for v≠0, so θ̂=(X′X)−1X′y is unique. Its residuals satisfy X′ê=0; with an intercept, they sum to zero. These sample identities hold regardless of whether the factor model prices anything.

With an intercept and nonconstant y, R²=1−SSE/SST measures the fraction of centered sample squared variation fitted. A large R² neither forces α̂=0 nor establishes that E[ε|f]=0, that the chosen factors are causal, or that future parameters will remain stable. The textbook disturbance estimate s²=SSE/(T−K−1) needs positive degrees of freedom; interpreting it as an unbiased noise-variance estimator additionally requires the relevant linear conditional-mean and homoskedastic error assumptions. It is not an alpha standard error by itself. Under Cov(ε|X)=σ²I, coefficient covariance is σ²(X′X)−1; replacing σ² by s² still needs inference assumptions and does not repair selection or nonstationarity.

Use numerical QR or other stable methods for realistic floating-point panels; the small lab solves exact rational normal equations so rounding does not hide rank. Exact full rank does not guarantee informative estimates when factor columns are nearly collinear. Measurement error in factors or estimated betas, stale prices, serial dependence and changing exposures require further analysis. The primary projection reference and the earlier regression chapter supply the least-squares geometry.

Omitting a factor changes what the included coefficient and intercept describe. Suppose the full population projection is y=α+β1f1+β2f2+ε, with ε orthogonal to both factors. Regressing only on an intercept and f1 gives

β̃1=β1+β2Cov(f1,f2)/Var(f1),
α̃=α+β2{E[f2]−[Cov(f1,f2)/Var(f1)]E[f1]}.

To prove the first equation, take Cov(f1,y) and divide by Var(f1)>0; the residual term vanishes by the stated orthogonality. The second follows by matching means. The same equations hold exactly in a full-rank finite sample when means and centered cross-products replace population moments and the full-model residual is orthogonal to the sample factors. An intercept can change sign after a factor is added without any manager decision or cash flow changing.

6. A cross-sectional risk premium answers another question

Time-series regressions estimate exposures from how each asset moves across dates. A cross-sectional calculation asks whether assets with different exposures have different average returns. For N test assets, collect the K estimated exposure columns in B and their evaluation-period mean excess returns in μ̂. With no free intercept under the maintained known-safe-rate, zero-alpha restriction, least squares solves

λ̂=(B′B)−1B′μ̂,   â=μ̂−Bλ̂,   B′â=0,

provided B has full column rank. A weighted criterion would change both formula and emphasis. Adding a free cross-sectional intercept changes the hypothesis; it is not an automatic estimate of the already-subtracted safe return. The residual â is a pricing error relative to the specified estimated-exposure relation, not a separately traded riskless payoff.

For traded factors in an exact population model, the risk prices equal their expected excess payoffs. In finite data, a cross-sectional estimate need not equal the factor sample means. Estimated first-stage betas carry error into the second stage; omitted factors, sampling variation, dependence, chosen test assets and a false zero-alpha restriction can all matter. Fitting N means with K exposures is also not a full model test. If N=K and B is invertible, arbitrary means can be matched exactly; there are no overidentifying mean restrictions in that fit.

A period-by-period second pass instead regresses each date's cross-section on previously estimated betas, producing λ̂t, then averages those estimates. With identical fixed B and identical asset coverage, linearity makes its average equal to (B′B)−1B′r̄. Changing B, coverage or weights breaks that simple identity. Even in the fixed case, uncertainty concerns a time series of estimates and estimated regressors; it cannot be read from the cross-sectional residual sum of squares alone. More advanced inference belongs to the later econometrics sequence. Fama and French's 2004 methodological discussion provides a dated primary route into estimated-beta and pricing-test limitations, not new evidence about today's premiums.

Worked example 3 — Fit, omitted factors and a second-pass estimate

Construct eight synthetic monthly observations by taking every combination x,z,h∈{−1,+1} once. These signs merely generate a transparent dataset. Let f1=0.01+0.02x, f2=0.015+0.01x+0.02z, and y=0.002+1.25f1−0.5f2+0.005h. All series are excess-return units for this sample; this is not the preceding one-period pricing economy.

The centered signs are mutually orthogonal and sum to zero. Thus the complete regression has α̂=0.002, β̂1=1.25, β̂2=−0.5 and residual 0.005h. Its SSE is 8×0.005²=1/5000. Since y−ȳ=0.02x−0.01z+0.005h, SST=8(0.02²+0.01²+0.005²)=21/5000. R² is 20/21≈95.2381%; the residual mean square with five degrees of freedom is 1/25000. No confidence level is attached to this artificial sign pattern.

Omitting f2 changes the slope by −0.5×(0.02×0.01/0.02²)=−0.25, giving β̃1=1. The sample mean of y is 0.002+1.25×0.01−0.5×0.015=0.007, so α̃=0.007−0.01=−0.003. Its residual is −0.01z+0.005h, SSE=1/1000 and R²=16/21. The model-dependent intercept moves from −0.3% to +0.2%; neither value alone proves skill, causal compensation or an investable opportunity.

Now consider a separate four-asset diagnostic cross-section. Prior-window estimated exposures are supplied as rows (1,0), (0,1), (1,1), (2,−1); mean excess returns over the same eight evaluation months are (0.014,0.020,0.028,0.006). Treat B as fixed for this descriptive calculation. Then B′B=[[6,−1],[−1,3]], with determinant 17, and B′μ̂=(0.054,0.042). The no-free-intercept fit gives

λ̂=(0.012,0.018),   â=(0.002,0.002,−0.002,0).

Direct multiplication confirms B′â=0. These fitted risk prices differ from the first panel's factor means (0.01,0.015). That comparison is a diagnostic, not an assertion that these finite summaries constitute a population pricing law. The factor and test-asset means use the same evaluation window; their exposure estimates come from an earlier window. An actual study must preserve that separation, disclose weighting and assess uncertainty. Exact spanning and exact population means would impose the stronger equalities; supplied estimates do not establish those assumptions.

7. Build a factor from a decision rule, then fund it

A characteristic-sorted factor needs a dated, reproducible protocol: the eligible universe, characteristic definition and release date, breakpoints, weights, rebalancing rule, corporate-action and delisting treatment, cash/funding convention and trading-cost model. A balance-sheet date is not its publication date. A current constituent list applied retrospectively can discard failed firms. Revised macroeconomic data can reveal information unavailable to an original decision-maker. Store the vintage actually available, and make the trade date later than its release.

The distinction is concrete in Kenneth French's primary factor definitions: a market excess-return series and long-minus-short portfolio spreads have explicit underlying portfolio rules and dated equity/accounting inputs. Those definitions illustrate a documented construction. They do not imply that a research series equals a client's realized after-cost return. This chapter imports no observations, historical return claim or forecast from that library.

Let wt−1 have long weights summing to +1 and short weights to −1. The gross spread ft=Σwi,t−1Ri,t is a zero-cost payoff per reference notional before costs. It uses beginning weights, not a ranking formed from the returns it is about to earn. Gross risky exposure is two per reference CU even though the signed sum is zero. Collateral, stock-borrow availability, rebates, funding spreads, execution, impact and margin policy determine whether an investor can hold it.

Actual turnover is based on quantities: with pre-trade shares nold, target shares nnew and current prices P, traded cash volume is ΣPi|ninew−niold|. A proportional one-way cost κ times that volume counts both buys and sells. The phrase “turnover” is also used for half that volume divided by capital; define the convention before multiplying by a cost rate. Comparing target weights alone can omit the drift of old holdings.

A fixed notional strategy does not automatically reinvest its profit into larger positions. Its factor payoffs should be summed as cash at that fixed scale. Account simple returns instead divide each net period profit by that period's opening equity; those returns compound to the final account wealth. External additions, withdrawals or financing changes would require their own ledger. A zero-cost factor spread has no well-defined simple return obtained by dividing by its zero initial cost.

Worked example 4 — A research spread becomes an account

In a separate four-month Ilex record, assets A–D start at price 100 and pay no distributions. An account begins with 100 CU collateral. At each month start, rank the four already-available distinct signals; buy 50 CU of each of the top two assets and short 50 CU of each of the bottom two. Keep the long and short reference notionals fixed at 100 each. Short proceeds can fund the longs; cash earns zero; there are no taxes or intramonth margin calls in this synthetic contract. Trading costs are 0.1% of every CU bought or sold, including final liquidation. Borrowing each month's 100 CU short position costs another 0.1 CU, paid at that month end. These are stipulated costs, not market estimates.

Total traded volume is 1,010, giving trade cost 1.01; total borrow cost is 0.40. Final positions are zero and final cash is 100+11−1.01−0.40=109.59. The investor's cumulative return is 9.59%. The actual monthly account returns are 3.2%, 1279/41280, 1479/42559 and −101/22019; compounding their growth factors recovers 1.0959. They are not the fixed-notional factor series.

Illegally sorting each month by its own subsequent returns would give hindsight gross spreads 3.5%,3.5%,4%,3%, averaging 3.5% instead of the feasible rule's 2.75%. This calculation exposes unavailable information; it is not an alternative backtest. Four synthetic months cannot establish persistence or statistical significance. The ledger also assumes executable shorts and no intervening margin calls; actual capacity would require additional evidence, prices and financing terms.

8. Design an empirical claim that can fail

Separate a model's role before fitting it. A descriptive model summarizes contemporaneous exposures. A forecasting model needs predictors measurable before the return and genuinely later evaluation data. A pricing model restricts expected returns through an economic SDF or justified approximation. An implementation study adds quantities, costs and constraints. Good performance in one role does not certify the others.

For a factor-pricing study, state the factor universe and economic mechanism, explain the test assets and return units, and define the estimation and evaluation windows before examining the desired result. Keep all eligible entries and exits, including adverse terminal returns, subject to a documented missing-data rule. Record searches across specifications. Evaluate stability on data not used to select factors or breakpoints, and assess serial and cross-asset dependence with methods appropriate to the research design. A larger model weakly improves in-sample fit by nesting; it need not improve external prediction or make a priced-factor interpretation more credible.

Residual correlation is useful diagnostic evidence. If many supposedly idiosyncratic residuals move together, the diversification premise may fail and a missing common exposure is plausible. That pattern alone does not identify its economic source. Likewise, adding a factor constructed from the very test asset can absorb its intercept mechanically. Ask whether the factor definition predates the test, can be implemented and prices other relevant assets under an independently defensible hypothesis. The successor chapters study efficiency, selection and performance evaluation; they retain these measurement and pricing distinctions.

9. Reproduce the Ilex analysis

Download the synthetic inputs, standard-library Python analysis, complete preserved output, integrity manifest and execution and scope guide into one folder. Run python3 v09-c06-analysis.py. No network, account or package installation is needed. Monetary amounts and most statistics are exact rational strings; the named square-root bound is a finite float. JSON null for a no-intercept R² means that the usual centered intercept-based statistic was deliberately not reported.

Reconstruct a result before reading the reference. Enumerate the pricing states and check every priced payoff, prove the product-kernel identity, verify regression normal equations using independent centered sums, and reconcile trading cash from shares and prices. In an input copy, change the clone price, residual scale, a sample outcome or a cost rate and predict the affected output. The README defines the allowed numerical edits and guarded conventions. The program is a small exact teaching model, not a general portfolio platform, data vendor or empirical-inference package.

Exercises

Give units, dates and the trading or statistical assumptions behind each answer. A pricing conclusion needs more than a fitted coefficient. For the open audit, credit explicit hypotheses and implementable repairs, not a preferred factor model.

  1. Replication at another quote. Two unit-price factor funds have excess payoffs f1,f2 with physical means 4% and 2.5%; the safe gross return is 1.04. A nonnegative terminal claim has exact payoff X=1.04+1.25f1+0.5f2. Derive its replica and fair price, and its expected simple return at that price. If an identical clone is quoted at 1.03, give all positions in a zero-initial-cost arbitrage and its sure payoff. Also compute the clone's expected simple return at its quoted price, explaining why the same payoff has a different return.
  2. A nontraded factor's normalization. Independent equiprobable signs U,V define m=(1−0.2U+0.1V)/1.05 and nontraded z=2U, measured in percentage points of a fictional macro surprise. A unit-price claim has excess payoff μ+0.03z+0.02V. Find the λ for z, its residual-pricing contribution and the μ required by the SDF. Show positivity of m and distinguish λ from E[z]. Rescale the factor to z*=10z; give the new coefficient and risk price and verify the unchanged premium.
  3. A conditional APT bound. A factor-neutral zero-cost position averages 100 uncorrelated zero-mean residuals, each with standard deviation 15%, and has constant mean payoff 0.5% per reference notional. Assume a pricing kernel with σ(m)/E[m]≤0.2. Compute the residual variance and bound on the absolute mean. Identify what is inconsistent. If each residual instead also contains the same independent 3% sign shock, recompute the bound. In the original finite independent-sign version, give one loss state and explain why the variance calculation alone is not sure arbitrage.
  4. A changed response, unchanged factor observations. Use Worked example 3's eight rows and replace y by y*=y+0.006+0.75f2. Without fitting software, derive the complete regression coefficients and residuals, SSE and R². Derive the intercept and slope after omitting f2. Explain why these changes are algebraic results for a constructed sample, not evidence that a new manager generated skill.
  5. A redundant second factor. Keep the original y and f1 in Worked example 3, but replace the second regressor by g=3f1−0.02. Derive the full set of coefficient triples (a,b,c) producing the OLS fitted values a+bf1+cg. Give two different triples, their common residual SSE and the reason a three-column full-rank solver should reject this specification. Does adding a label provide another independently identified risk?
  6. Second-pass sensitivity. Keep the four-row B and four mean returns in Worked example 3. Increase only the first asset's mean return by 0.004, holding the supplied prior-window betas fixed. Derive the change in λ̂, the new coefficients and all four new pricing residuals. Verify B′â=0. Does this force the separately observed factor means to change? Explain what the disagreement can and cannot establish.
  7. Trade actual quantities. A separate two-asset account starts with 100 cash, zero holdings and asset prices 100. In Period 1 it targets +100 CU of A and −100 of B; returns are 10% and 5%. Before Period 2 it reverses to −100 A and +100 B; subsequent returns are −4% and 2%, then all positions are liquidated. Long and short notionals stay fixed at 100. Short proceeds are reusable, cash earns zero, no intraperiod margin call occurs, one-way trading cost is 0.2% of cash volume and borrow cost is 0.1 CU each period. Compute initial, rebalance and liquidation volumes; both gross cash profits; all costs; and final cash. Explain the error in using only target-weight changes for the rebalance.
  8. Referee the factor claim. A report selects the best of 400 factor specifications on one sample, sorts Month 1 holdings using a macro release first available in Month 2, drops firms that later delist, and calls a centered nontraded shock's zero mean its zero risk price. It then constructs an extra factor from the tested fund's own return and treats perfect fit as proof of a priced, investable premium. Identify each distinct failure. Design a revised study that separates exposure estimation, pricing, prediction and implementation, and state what evidence could change your conclusion. No outside market data or preferred factor list is required.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Hold 1.25 Fund 1, 0.5 Fund 2 and −0.75 safe units; cost is 1 and payoff is exactly X. Expected excess return is 1.25×0.04+0.5×0.025=0.0625, so expected simple total return is 0.1025. Short one clone at 1.03, buy 1.25 and 0.5 fund units, and hold −0.72 safe units: the replica's −0.75 plus the invested 0.03 receipt. Initial cost −1.03+1.25+0.5−0.72=0; payoff is 0.03×1.04=0.0312 in every state. The clone's mean payoff is 1.1025, hence its quoted-price return is 1.1025/1.03−1=29/412≈7.038835%. Return normalization changes with the price; the exact same payoff, rather than the same numerical beta at a different price, supports the arbitrage.

  2. The smallest kernel numerator is 0.7>0. E[z]=0, but Cov(m,z)=−0.4/1.05, so λ=0.4 percentage points. The residual ε=0.02V has Cov(m,ε)=0.002/1.05, giving residual-pricing contribution −0.002. Thus μ=0.03×0.4−0.002=0.01. Under z*=10z, b*=0.003 and λ*=4 in the rescaled factor units, so b*λ*=0.012 remains unchanged and the total excess mean is still 1%. Zero statistical mean does not imply zero covariance risk price; the nontraded factor is not a traded excess-return payoff.

  3. The average residual variance is 0.15²/100=0.000225, with standard deviation 0.015. The stated kernel bound allows at most 0.2×0.015=0.003, below the supplied 0.005 mean. That combination of exact mean, residual structure, zero-cost pricing and bounded kernel is inconsistent; the calculation does not tell which empirical assumption would fail. With the common independent shock, variance becomes 0.03²+0.000225=0.001125, so the bound rises to 0.2√0.001125≈0.006708204, which does not rule out 0.005. In the independent ±0.15 residual version, all signs negative produce payoff 0.005−0.15=−0.145 with positive probability 2−100. A small variance alone does not remove that loss state.

  4. Substituting y* gives complete coefficients (0.008,1.25,0.25). The residual remains 0.005h, so SSE remains 1/5000. Centered y* is 0.0275x+0.005z+0.005h; SST=8(0.0275²+0.005²+0.005²)=129/20000, giving R²=125/129. The short-regression slope is 1.25+0.25×0.5=11/8; its intercept is 0.008+0.25(0.015−0.5×0.01)=21/2000. These follow from the stipulated addition to the same outcome. They neither identify an economic shock's price nor establish a manager's implementable contribution.

  5. The fitted expression becomes (a−0.02c)+(b+3c)f1. The unique fitted line from the one-factor regression therefore requires a−0.02c=−0.003 and b+3c=1. Every real c gives a=−0.003+0.02c and b=1−3c. Examples are (−0.003,1,0) and (0.007,−0.5,0.5). Both yield the same residual −0.01z+0.005h and SSE 1/1000. The intercept/factor columns are dependent, so X′X is singular and the separate triple is unidentified. Rejecting the full-rank solve is appropriate; it does not mean the fitted values are impossible. Relabeling a linear combination adds no new factor span.

  6. B′Δμ̂=(0.004,0) and (B′B)−1=(1/17)[[3,1],[1,6]], so Δλ̂=(3/4250,1/4250). Adding this to (0.012,0.018) gives (27/2125,31/1700). Subtracting the newly fitted means from (0.018,0.020,0.028,0.006) gives (9/1700,3/1700,−1/340,−1/850). The first normal-equation sum is 9/1700−1/340−2/850=0; the second is 3/1700−1/340+1/850=0. The factor observations did not change, so their sample means do not change. This sensitivity is compatible with several estimation or model explanations; it does not establish statewise arbitrage or force a population premium to equal either estimate.

  7. Initial volume is 200, costing 0.4. Period 1 gross profit is 100×0.10−100×0.05=5; after 0.1 borrow cost, equity is 104.5. Old signed holdings are (110,−105). Reversing to (−100,100) requires volume 210+205=415, costing 0.83. Period 2 gross profit is (−100)(−0.04)+100×0.02=6. Ending holdings before closing are (−96,102), so liquidation volume is 198, costing 0.396. Total trade cost is 1.626 and total borrow cost 0.2. Final positions are zero; cash is 100+5+6−1.626−0.2=109.174, a cumulative investor return of 9.174%. A target-weight-only volume of 400 ignores drift and understates the rebalance cost by 15×0.002=0.03.

  8. Selection among 400 specifications changes the interpretation of an unadjusted best-result statistic; preserve search history and reserve genuinely unexamined evaluation data. The Month 2 release is unavailable for the Month 1 trade; use the last vintage actually known before each decision and model a valid release-to-execution lag. Dropping later delistings conditions on future survival; reconstruct the eligible universe and terminal outcomes without outcome-driven exclusions. E[z]=0 is a centering statement, while λ=−RfCov(z,m) can be nonzero. A factor built from the outcome can produce mechanical fit; it needs independent economic justification, availability and evaluation on other assets to support a pricing interpretation.

    A satisfactory revised design separately specifies the exposure regression, SDF or beta-pricing restriction, forecast information set and executable portfolio. It fixes asset coverage, units, dates, funding, short availability, cost assumptions and evaluation rules; handles missing observations without hiding losses; evaluates dependence and estimated-beta uncertainty; and reports alternative explanations rather than selecting a desired story. Evidence that could change a skeptical conclusion includes a reproducible predeclared result on genuinely new data, robust pricing restrictions across relevant assets, an economically defensible kernel and viable after-cost holdings. These remain distinct pieces of evidence, not a guarantee of future returns. Grade all five identified failures and a coherent repair connecting information, estimation, pricing and implementation; no specific factor list is required.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach a colleague why Claim A's misquoted clone permits exact arbitrage while Claim B's positive factor alpha does not. Write both hedged terminal payoffs and explain which equality is statewise and which is a covariance restriction. Then explain why a mean spread per fixed notional is not automatically a compounded client return.

Teach-back benchmark

The clone and replica have the same full payoff, so buying the cheaper payoff and investing the difference leaves 0.0204 in every state at zero initial cost. Claim B instead leaves 0.004+0.04E after its traded factors are hedged, including a −0.036 state. Its factor-orthogonal residual covaries with the positive pricing kernel, exactly supporting its 0.004 alpha. A factor spread is normalized by reference notional; the investor must supply a funded account. Fixed-notional profits are added as cash, whereas actual account returns divide net profit by opening equity and compound through that changing equity. An explanation that drops the residual, the safe payoff or the account denominator needs repair.

After one week without notes: (1) an exactly spanned asset has traded-factor exposures (2,−1) and factor means (2%,3%); give its expected excess return; (2) a two-factor projection has β1=1.5, β2=−0.4 and Cov(f1,f2)/Var(f1)=0.5; give the omitted-factor slope; (3) 36 equally weighted uncorrelated residuals each have standard deviation 6%, with uniform SDF coefficient-of-variation bound 0.25; give the absolute-alpha bound; (4) explain why a centered nontraded factor's zero mean does not determine its risk price.

Retention answers

(1) 2×2%−3%=1%, conditional on the exact spanning/trading assumptions. (2) 1.5−0.4×0.5=1.3. (3) Residual standard deviation is 0.06/√36=0.01, giving bound 0.0025=0.25%; finite residual risk need not vanish. (4) λ=−RfCov(z,m), which centering does not change. Equality with an expected factor payoff requires the additional traded zero-cost normalization.

Sources and further study

The linked primary teaching, methodological and factor-provider sources have narrow recorded scopes. All state laws, sample observations, ledgers, derivations and problems here are original. This chapter proves exact finite spanning and one sufficient approximate-pricing bound; it does not establish all versions of infinite-market APT or validate any empirical factor zoo. Continue through the successor chapters on efficiency and performance before interpreting a research factor as evidence of skill. Later planned financial econometrics material develops the inference needed for more demanding empirical claims.

Sources and further study

  • MIT OpenCourseWare — Projection Matrices and Least Squares — Further study of orthogonal projections and least-squares geometry. The library uses original examples and problems.
  • Eugene F. Fama and Kenneth R. French — The Capital Asset Pricing Model: Theory and Evidence (2004) — Primary author paper on the market portfolio/proxy problem, regression pricing restrictions, hypothesis interpretation and implementation limits. The chapter treats the paper's empirical assessment as dated 2004, not current market evidence.
  • Andrew W. Lo, MIT 15.401 — Lectures 15–17: The CAPM and APT (Fall 2008), scoped APT discussion — Primary teaching route for multiple systematic factors, linear pricing restrictions and the need to specify factors; this chapter supplies its own finite-state exact-spanning proof and a separate conditional diversification bound.
  • Kenneth R. French Data Library — Description of Fama/French Factors, scoped construction definitions — Primary factor-provider illustration of a traded market excess-return series, long-minus-short portfolio spreads, stated size/book-equity inputs and calendar construction. No downloaded performance observations or evidence of a future premium are used.
